check:0:1.q: Why not “The problem goes away, because the fact fits mo…”?
check:0:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. A bigger **context window** (the most tokens a model can read in one call) does let more text fit. Your agent would hit the hard limit later in the run.

But fitting was never the problem. The question says the right fact is *already in the prompt*. So the fact fits fine. The answers still get worse.

That drop is **context rot**: answers get worse as the prompt gets longer, even when the right fact is there. It comes from length, not from running out of room. The lesson is clear that a model with a bigger window does not fix it. Your prompt would be just as long as before, so the slip would still happen.

The real fix is to keep the prompt short and useful. Measure each call's fill, clean up old tool results when it passes a line like 80 percent, and pick fewer, better chunks.

"It still slips as the prompt grows, so keep the context short" is better because it names the real cause, length, and points to the fix that actually helps.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only small gap is that 'fill' and 'tool results' are used without a definition, but the answer is accurate, on topic, under 200 words, and contains no solution code.

check:0:2.q: Why not “It slips sooner, because bigger windows read le…”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. It does not expect the bigger window to fix the problem, and the lesson agrees. A bigger window does not cure **context rot**, the drop in answer quality as the prompt gets longer.

Where it goes wrong is the reason it gives. The lesson never says bigger windows read less carefully, or that they slip sooner. The cause of context rot is the length of the prompt you actually send, not the size of the window.

Think of the window as the size of a bucket. A bigger bucket does not make the water worse. It just lets you pour in more before it overflows. A run with a twice-as-big window can keep growing its history for longer. As the prompt grows, answers still get worse, much as before.

So the "slips sooner" option blames the wrong thing. It points you at the model's window, when the thing to watch is each call's fill: its input tokens as a percent of the window.

"It still slips as the prompt grows, so keep the context short" is better because it names the real cause and gives the fix that works.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Keep going until it hits the limit”?
check:1:0.a:
"Keep going until it hits the limit" gets one thing right. At 85 percent the call still fits. Nothing has broken yet, so the run could carry on for now.

But it misses three things.

First, quality is already slipping. Remember **context rot**: answers get worse as the prompt gets longer, even when the right fact is in there. At 85 percent, the model is reading a lot of old, noisy text.

Second, the fill only goes up. The agent resends its whole history on every call. In the lesson's example, each call added about 30,000 tokens. From 85 percent, one more call could jump past 100 percent.

Third, hitting the limit means failure. The call errors out, or text gets cut off, often in the middle of a task. Then you lose work.

The 80 percent line is an early warning. It gives you room to act before trouble arrives.

Clean up, like clearing old tool results, is right because it shrinks the prompt now, while the run still has room. That keeps answers sharp and the run safely under the limit.

judge.notes: Minor: the closing 'better answer' part runs to two sentences instead of one, and the 'call errors out or text is cut off' detail goes slightly beyond the lesson, though it does not contradict it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Switch to a model with a bigger window”?
check:1:1.a:
A bigger window gets one thing right. It gives the run more room, so call 12 would no longer be near the limit. The **window** is the most tokens a model can read in one call.

It misses the real problem, in two ways.

First, **context rot**. Answers get worse as the prompt gets longer, even when the right fact is in it. A bigger window does not fix that. The prompt is just as long and just as cluttered, so answers can still slip.

Second, the growth keeps going. An agent sends its whole history again on every call, so each call reads more than the last. With a bigger window, the fill still climbs call after call. You only reach the line later, then face the same choice.

So the 80 percent line is a signal to act on the prompt itself, not to find a bigger container.

The right answer is to clean up, for example by clearing old tool results. That shrinks the prompt, which keeps the model's answers sharp and makes room for the calls still to come.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Add more chunks so nothing is missed”?
check:2:1.a:
"Add more chunks so nothing is missed" gets one thing right. Missing the fact you need is a real risk. A **chunk** is one piece of retrieved text, and if the right chunk never gets retrieved, the model can't use it.

But this prompt already has 50 chunks. The fact is probably in there. The problem is that the model doesn't use it well. Remember **context rot**: answers get worse as the prompt gets longer, even when the right fact is present. Adding more chunks makes the prompt longer, so it makes this problem worse, not better.

More chunks also fill the context window faster. That brings each call closer to the limit and makes cleanup needed sooner.

The lesson points the other way. Fewer, better chunks often win. You can test this by comparing eval scores for 5 chunks against 50.

"Put the question after the chunks" is better because it moves the question to the end of the prompt, where models pay the most attention. It also costs no extra tokens.

judge.notes: Minor: 'costs no extra tokens' and 'the fact is probably in there' go beyond the lesson, and the closing explanation runs to two sentences instead of one, but nothing contradicts the lesson.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Send the chunks in a random order”?
check:2:2.a:
Shuffling the chunks gets one thing right. It notices that **where** text sits in the prompt matters. A chunk is one piece of retrieved text, and models do pay more attention to some spots than others.

But shuffling misses the real problem. The question is still at the very top, the spot farthest from the end, where models pay the most attention. After reading 50 chunks, the model has to reach all the way back to remember what it was asked. Random order doesn't move the question at all.

Shuffling also leaves the result to luck. The most useful chunk might land near the end one time and in the middle the next. Your eval scores (the measured quality of answers on test questions) would jump around from run to run. That makes it hard to tell if anything really improved.

So "Put the question after the chunks" is the better first change. It places the question at the end, where the model pays the most attention, right before it starts to answer.

judge.notes: Passes, but the phrase "the spot farthest from the end, where models pay the most attention" could be misread as saying the top gets the most attention; rewording it would help beginners.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that context fill is going unwatched**

- **Answers get worse late in a run.** Early steps are sharp. Later steps miss facts that are in the prompt, repeat work, or drift from the goal. That is context rot: quality drops as the prompt grows.
- **Short tests pass, long tasks fail.** Your evals use quick, few-step tasks and score well. Real users run long tasks, and the scores fall.
- **Sudden hard errors.** A run crashes with a "context length exceeded" style message. Nobody saw it coming because nobody tracked the fill.
- **Input tokens climb on every call.** In your traces, each model call reads more than the last, and nothing ever trims it.
- **More chunks, worse scores.** Retrieving 50 chunks scores lower than 5, yet the prompt keeps the 50.

**Quickest check**

Open one long run's trace in MLflow. Look at each chat model call, which MLflow calls a *span* (one step in the trace). Note its input tokens. Divide by your model's window and see where the fill first passes 80 percent. If that point lines up with where answers start slipping, you have found the problem.

judge.notes: Minor: 'evals' is not explained, and the 50-versus-5 chunks sign is stated more firmly than the lesson's 'often beat more'. Neither is serious enough to fail.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the rule needs extra care.

**One agent, several models.** Some agents use a small, cheap model for easy steps and a bigger one for hard steps. Each model has its own window, so one fixed `WINDOW` gives a wrong fill for some calls. Look up the window for the model each call actually used.

**Token counts go missing.** Some providers, or some streaming setups (where the reply arrives piece by piece), don't report `input_tokens`. The `if use` check then skips those calls quietly, and a nearly full call can go unseen. Count how many calls had no usage data, and treat that as a warning, not as "fine."

**The line is too late.** Context rot can hurt answers well before 80 percent, especially on hard questions. A fixed line is only a starting guess. Run your evals at a few fill levels, see where scores start to drop, and set your cleanup line just before that point.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only slightly unsupported detail is 'especially on hard questions', which the lesson does not state but also does not contradict.

learn:term.a:
A **context window** is the most text a model can read in one call. It is measured in **tokens**, which are small chunks of text, often a word or part of a word.

Think of a desk. Everything the model needs for one answer must fit on the desk at once: your question, the chat history, and any retrieved documents. The window is the size of that desk. If the pile gets bigger than the desk, it no longer fits, and the call fails or gets cut off.

In the lesson's example, the first line sets the desk size:

```
window: 128000 tokens
```

Each call then shows how many tokens it sent, and what percent of the window that is. Call 0 uses 12,000 tokens, which is 9 percent. By call 3 it uses 108,000 tokens, which is 84 percent. The pile grows because an agent resends its whole history on every call.

In the MLflow code, `WINDOW = 128000` holds that same limit, so each call's tokens can be turned into a percent.

One catch: even when everything fits, a fuller desk still gives worse answers. That drop is called context rot.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that the call 'fails or gets cut off' goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes, it sees the same calls coming back”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. The calls really do come back: A shows up again and again, and so does B.

But the check doesn't ask "have I seen this call before?" It asks "is this call the same as the one just before it?" It only counts repeats **in a row**.

Walk through the trace:

```
A   # count starts at 1
B   # different from A, count goes back to 1
A   # different from B, back to 1
B   # back to 1 again
```

The count never gets past 1, so it never reaches 3. The check never fires. The agent loops forever while the guardrail sees nothing wrong. Looking back over the last three calls fails the same way: A, B, A are not all the same.

So the repeat check only catches one kind of loop. A smarter agent can get stuck in a pattern it was never built to spot.

"No, so you also need a total step limit" is better because a cap like `recursion_limit` of 25 stops the run after a fixed number of steps, whatever shape the loop takes.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Only if you lower the limit to 2 calls”?
check:0:2.a:
**Why lowering the limit doesn't help**

The idea has one thing right. A smaller limit catches a true repeat sooner. With a limit of 2, `search('weather paris')` twice in a row would stop the run one call earlier.

But look at the pattern A, B, A, B. No call is ever followed by the same call. Each time, the "repeats in a row" count goes back to 1. So it never reaches 2, or 3, or any number above 1.

A limit of 1 is no fix either. Every single call would "match," so the check would stop every agent on its first step.

A limit of 2 also has a cost. Real agents sometimes retry a call once, for example after a brief network error. A limit of 2 would stop those healthy runs too.

**Why the other answer is better**

"No, so you also need a total step limit" is better because a cap on total steps, such as `recursion_limit` set to 25, stops any loop, whatever its pattern, once the agent has taken too many steps.

judge.notes: No real failures. Minor nitpicks: the network-retry point is not from the lesson, and "every call would match" for a limit of 1 is loose, since the first call has nothing before it to match.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Leave the default, it stops in time”?
check:1:0.a:
"Leave the default, it stops in time" gets one thing right. LangGraph does have a built-in step cap, called `recursion_limit`. A "step" is one move through the graph, like the model thinking once or a tool running once. So a stuck agent will not run forever.

The problem is how late it stops. In langgraph 1.2.11 the default is 10,007 steps. A looping agent can repeat the same tool call thousands of times before it hits that cap. Each step can cost tokens (the pieces of text the model reads and writes, which you pay for), time and money. The question even tells you what happened: the agent ran for hours. That is the default "working." It technically stopped, but far too late to be useful.

A guardrail should stop a bad run early, before it does damage. A huge default does not do that.

"Pass your own small limit, like 25" is better because it stops a stuck agent after a few wasted steps instead of thousands:

```python
graph.invoke(inputs, config={"recursion_limit": 25})
```

check:1:2.q: Why not “Set it higher so the run can finish”?
check:1:2.a:
"Set it higher so the run can finish" assumes the agent was close to done and just needed more room. In this story, it wasn't. It was **stuck**, meaning it kept repeating itself without making progress. A stuck agent never finishes, however many steps you allow.

There's also a problem with the number. You never set `recursion_limit`, so LangGraph used its default. In langgraph 1.2.11 that default is 10,007 steps. That's why the run went on for hours. Raising it further only lets the loop run longer, which costs more time and more tokens. Tokens are the chunks of text the model reads and writes, and you pay for each one.

The option does get one thing right. Some real tasks need more steps than others, so a limit can sometimes be too tight. But that isn't what happened here.

**Pass your own small limit, like 25** is better because it stops a stuck agent within a few steps instead of hours, so a loop stays cheap and you find out quickly.

```python
graph.invoke(inputs, config={"recursion_limit": 25})
```

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that some real tasks need more steps goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it does not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Restart the run from the beginning”?
check:2:0.a:
Restarting gets one thing right. A fresh run starts clean, so any confusion from the first attempt is gone.

But it misses the bigger problem. The run hit its **token cap**, the limit on how much text the model may read and write. (A **token** is a small chunk of a word.) Restarting changes nothing about the task or the cap. So the new run will likely burn through the same budget and stop at the same spot. You pay twice and get nothing back.

It also throws away the work already done. Halfway through, the agent may have found useful facts. A restart deletes them.

And the model never learns what happened. From its side, the run just vanished. It can't adjust, because it was never told there was a limit.

**"Tell the model why it was stopped"** is better because the model can then wrap up with what it has, such as a partial answer or a clear note that it ran out of budget, instead of failing silently or repeating the same costly path.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Raise the cap and carry on quietly”?
check:2:1.a:
"Raise the cap and carry on quietly" gets one thing right. Sometimes a task really does need more room, and a bigger cap can be a fair fix. A **token** is a small chunk of text the model reads or writes. You pay for every one, so a token cap is a spending limit.

But raising the cap automatically, every time it is hit, means there is no real limit at all. The cap exists to stop a run that is burning money. If the agent is stuck repeating itself, a bigger cap just lets it waste more before it stops again.

"Quietly" is the second problem. Nobody learns anything. The model doesn't know it ran out, so it can't wrap up, summarise what it found, or explain what is left. You don't see it in your logs either, so you can't spot that this task keeps hitting the limit. A **log** is the record your system writes about each run.

The right answer is "Tell the model why it was stopped." It turns a sudden cut-off into a clear signal, so the model can end with a useful partial answer instead of nothing.

judge.notes: No check fails. The points about logs and a task sometimes needing a bigger cap come from outside the lesson but do not contradict it, and the closing explanation runs to two sentences instead of one.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that loop guardrails are missing or broken**

**In your traces.** A trace is the step-by-step record of one agent run. Look for the same tool call, with the same arguments, appearing again and again. For example, `search('weather paris')` three, ten or fifty times in a row.

**In your numbers.**
- A few runs use far more steps, tokens or seconds than the rest.
- Your token bill jumps with no matching rise in users.
- Some runs end with a recursion error after thousands of steps. That means the default limit of 10,007 was the only thing that stopped them.

**In your results.** Users wait a long time and then get no answer, or a vague one.

**Signs the guardrail is built wrong.**
- It never fires, even on obvious loops. A common cause is comparing each call's `id`, which is unique every time, so no two calls ever match.
- It stops healthy runs too early, such as after two different searches.

**Quickest check.** Sort recent runs by step count. Open the longest one and read its tool calls. Then confirm your `invoke` call passes a small `recursion_limit`, such as 25.

learn:stops.a:
The "repeats in a row" rule is a good first guardrail. Here are three cases where it needs help.

**The agent rewords its call.** It might try `search('weather paris')`, then `search('Paris weather')`, then `search('weather in paris')`. Each call is different text, so the exact match never fires. Add a per-tool budget instead, such as "no more than 5 searches per run, whatever the arguments."

**The agent alternates between calls.** A pattern like A, B, A, B never repeats twice in a row, so the count keeps starting again at 1. Keep a small `recursion_limit` (the cap on total steps) as a backstop. You can also count how many times each exact call appears across the whole run.

**Repeating is actually correct.** Polling means checking the same thing again and again until it changes, like asking whether a Databricks job has finished. Here the same call is expected. Give that tool a higher limit, wait between checks, and cap the total time.

In every case, tell the model why it was stopped so it can change course.

judge.notes: Passes, with minor nits: each case runs four sentences instead of two or three, and the Databricks example is not from the lesson and is not explained.

learn:term.a:
Think of the guardrails along a mountain road. They don't steer the car. They only matter when something goes wrong, and then they stop the car before it goes over the edge.

For agents, a **guardrail** is a limit your code checks while the agent runs. The model still decides what to do next. The guardrail stops the run when the agent is clearly stuck or spending too much.

In the lesson's example, the trace shows `search('weather paris')` three times in a row. After the first call, nothing new is learned. The `route` function compares the tool name and arguments of each call. If the last three match, it returns `"stop"` instead of `"tools"`. That is the guardrail stepping in.

The second guardrail is `recursion_limit`, passed in `config`. It caps the total number of steps. It catches loops the repeat check misses, like an agent switching back and forth between two different calls. With a limit of 25, the run ends after 25 steps no matter what.

The lesson also mentions caps on tokens (the chunks of text a model reads and writes, which you pay for) and on time.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Fix the newest failure, then the one before it,…”?
check:0:1.a:
"Fix the newest failure first" has one thing going for it. Recent runs used the latest version of your agent, so their problems are probably still real. It also feels concrete, because you always know what to work on next.

But it sorts problems by *when* they happened, not by *how often* they happen. The newest failure might be a rare one that shows up in 3 of 300 runs. You could spend a whole day on it while a problem behind 100 other failures waits.

Going one by one also hides patterns. Ten failures might all be the same "repeated step" problem. Read separately, they look like ten different bugs, and you may fix the same thing several times. With 300 failures and one week, you won't reach the end of the list.

That's why the right answer is "Label a sample, count the labels, fix the biggest group." Labeling a sample of about 50 failures and counting the labels shows you which single fix will clear the most failures, so your week goes where it helps most.

judge.notes: The claim that recent runs used the latest agent version is not in the lesson, but it is hedged with 'probably' and does not contradict the lesson, so the answer passes.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Rewrite the whole system prompt, then rerun eve…”?
check:0:2.a:
Rewriting the system prompt is not a silly idea. The **system prompt** is the standing instruction the agent reads before every task, and sometimes it really is the cause. So the instinct to fix something is right.

The problem is that it's a guess. You haven't looked at why the runs failed. You might rewrite the prompt and miss the real problem, such as the agent repeating the same search over and over. A big rewrite also changes many things at once. If results get better or worse, you can't tell which change did it.

Rerunning every task is costly too. With 300 failures and one week, that time is better spent learning what went wrong.

Labeling gives you evidence. In the lesson's example, `repeated step` is the largest group, with 41 traces, ahead of `never stopped` with 22. That tells you where one fix pays off most. It also hands you trace ids like `t-193` to open and read.

Labeling a sample and counting the labels is better because it shows you which single problem causes the most failures, so your first fix targets real evidence instead of a hunch.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Let each person count their own”?
check:1:0.a:
"Let each person count their own" sounds fair, but it leaves the real problem in place.

**What it gets right:** each person probably uses their own words the same way every time. So inside one person's pile, the counts make some sense.

**What it misses:** the whole point of counting is to find the *biggest* problem across all failures. If one person writes "looped" and the other writes "kept repeating" for the same thing, that one problem gets split into two smaller piles. Say each pile has about 20. Neither looks like the top problem, even though together they might be 41 and clearly the biggest. You could end up fixing the wrong thing first.

It also breaks later steps. A search in MLflow for `feedback.failure_label = 'repeated step'` only finds traces with that exact name. And an LLM judge (a model that grades) can't learn to match "your" labels if there are two sets of names.

**Why "Agree on a fixed list of labels" is right:** when everyone picks from the same short list, one problem always gets one name, so the counts add up correctly and the biggest group is real.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that each person uses their own words consistently, and the claim that a judge can't learn from two label sets, are mild inferences the lesson doesn't state directly.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Use longer, more detailed labels”?
check:1:1.a:
Longer labels don't solve the real problem. The problem is that two people used **different names for the same thing**. When you count labels, the computer treats `looped` and `kept repeating` as two separate piles. Your biggest group gets split in half, and it might not look like the biggest anymore.

Making labels longer actually makes this worse. A long, detailed label gives people even more words to choose differently. One person writes "agent repeated the same search several times." Another writes "searched again and again without new results." Same problem, still two piles.

There is one thing that idea gets right: detail is useful. You want to know *why* a trace got its label. But that detail belongs in the `rationale` field (the short note explaining the label, like "Same search 4 times"). It doesn't belong in the label itself. The label should stay short and exact so counting works.

A fixed list of labels is better because everyone picks from the same names, like `repeated step`. Then the same problem always lands in the same pile, and the counts are true.

check:2:1.q: Why not “It labels faster than a person”?
check:2:1.a:
"It labels faster than a person" is true. Speed is the reason you want an LLM judge (a model that grades) in the first place. Labelling 500 traces by hand would take you days.

But speed is not something you need to check. You already know the judge is fast. The real question is whether its labels are right.

Think about what happens if they're wrong. Say the judge calls many "never stopped" traces "repeated step". Your counts now say "repeated step" is the biggest group. You spend your time fixing that, while the real top problem stays broken. A fast judge with bad labels just gives you wrong counts sooner.

Your 50 hand labels are your answer key. Run the judge on those same 50 and compare its label with yours on each trace. If they mostly agree, you can trust it on the next 500. If they don't, fix the judge's instructions first.

"Its labels match yours on the 50" is better because it checks that the judge is correct, and that is what makes its counts worth acting on.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. The claim that labelling 500 traces by hand would take 'days' is not from the lesson, but it is harmless and does not contradict it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “It uses more labels than you did”?
check:2:2.a:
"It uses more labels than you did" sounds like the judge is being more thorough. It isn't, and it can be a warning sign.

**What it gets right:** it pays attention to the judge's labels. That is the right thing to inspect before you trust it with 500 traces.

**What it misses:** the number of labels says nothing about whether the labels are *correct*. And the lesson asks you to use a **fixed list** of labels, so the same problem always gets the same name. A judge that adds extra labels breaks that rule. For example, it might call one problem "repeated step" in some traces and "looped search" in others. That one problem now sits in two smaller piles. Your counts shrink, and the real biggest group may no longer look biggest. You could end up fixing the wrong thing first.

**Why "Its labels match yours on the 50" is better:** your 50 hand labels are the known right answers, so if the judge gives the same label you did on those same traces, you have real evidence it will label the next 500 the way you would.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the only slight overreach is calling the 50 hand labels 'known right answers', where the lesson only treats them as the reference the judge must match.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Fixes keep landing, but the failure rate barely moves.** You may be fixing small, rare problems while the biggest group stays untouched.
- **The same problem has many names.** For example "loop", "repeated search" and "stuck again". Each name gets a small count, so the real biggest group is split up and hidden.
- **A huge "other" pile.** If most traces land there, your label list doesn't fit your failures.
- **Counts don't add up.** The labels total less than your sample, say 38 out of 50. Some traces were skipped.
- **The judge drifts.** The **LLM judge** (a model that grades) gives labels that differ from what a person would give on the same traces.
- **The top count doesn't shrink.** You fixed "repeated step", ran again, and it's still on top.

**Quickest check**

Pull the counts by label from MLflow. Confirm they add up to your sample size. Then open the two example ids for the top label and read them. If both clearly show that exact problem, your labels are working. If they don't, tighten your fixed label list and relabel before fixing anything.

judge.notes: No real problems. Two minor points: the 'other' pile idea goes beyond the lesson, and 'top count doesn't shrink' is a fix-failed sign rather than a skipped-idea sign. Checking only two example ids is also a thin test for 'labels are working'.

learn:stops.a:
**When does "label, count, fix the biggest pile" need extra care?**

**1. One trace fails in more than one way.**
A run might repeat a step *and* never stop. One label hides the second problem. Give each trace a main label, allow an optional second one, and count both.

**2. Your agent changes over time.**
After you fix the biggest pile, the mix of failures shifts, and new kinds may not fit your fixed list. Pull a fresh sample of failed traces after each fix. Add a new label only when several traces share a problem no current label covers.

**3. You have very few failures.**
With five failed runs, a count of 3 versus 2 tells you little. Read every trace closely instead, and treat the counts as hints, not a ranking.

Also watch the **LLM judge** (a model that grades). If you change your labels or your agent, check again that its labels still match a person's before trusting its counts.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the multi-label suggestion departs from the lesson's one-label rule, but that fits a question about when the rule changes.

learn:term.a:
A **taxonomy** is the general idea: a fixed list of categories you sort things into. Any field can have one. MAST is one specific taxonomy, built by researchers for one job: naming the common ways AI agents fail.

Think of a library. "A shelving system" is the general idea: every book goes in a set category. The Dewey Decimal System is one particular shelving system that many libraries use. Taxonomy is like "a shelving system." MAST is like Dewey.

**How they work together**

- The taxonomy idea says: use the same fixed names every time, so the same problem always lands in the same pile. That makes your counts trustworthy.
- MAST gives you a ready-made list to start from. It includes failures like repeating steps, not knowing when to stop, ignoring the task, and weak or missing checks.

In the lesson's example, the labels `repeated step`, `never stopped`, and `ignored task` match MAST's failure types. Because each failure gets one name from a fixed list, you can count them: 41, 22, 9. That tells you to fix `repeated step` first.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that the example labels match MAST's types is inferred rather than stated in the lesson, but it is reasonable and consistent.

check:0:0.a:
"4200 ms" is a real number from the trace. It is how long the `agent_run` span lasted from start to finish. So it gets that part right.

But the question asks how long the parent took **on its own**. A parent's time includes its children's time. The 4200 ms counts the time spent in `plan`, `tool:search` and `answer` too. Those children ran one after another, so their times add up: 600 + 3100 + 400 = 4100 ms.

Answering 4200 ms mixes the parent's own time with its children's time. That can mislead you when hunting for what's slow. It makes the parent look like the problem, when most of that time was really spent in a child, mostly `tool:search`.

A span's own time is what is left after you take its children away: 4200 − 4100 = 100 ms.

"100 ms" is better because it removes the children's time and keeps only the time that belongs to the parent alone.

check:0:2.a:
"8300 ms" comes from adding everything: 4200 + 600 + 3100 + 400. It gets one thing right. It sees that the children's times matter to the answer.

But it adds them when it should take them away. The parent's 4200 ms is measured from when the parent starts to when it ends. The children run during that window, so their time is already inside the 4200. Adding them again counts the same time twice.

Picture a 4200 ms box. The three children fill most of it: 600 + 3100 + 400 = 4100 ms. The question asks how much of the box is left over. That leftover is the parent's own time, the work it did itself, outside any child.

Also, "8300 ms" is longer than the whole run. A part of a run can never take longer than the run itself, so that is a good sign something went wrong.

"100 ms" is better because it starts from the parent's total and subtracts the children's time: 4200 − 4100 = 100 ms.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. The line "longer than the whole run" assumes the 4200 ms parent is the root, which the Check question doesn't say; "longer than the parent's own 4200 ms" would be safer.

check:1:1.a:
"Inside the plan span" gets one thing right. It looks *inside* a child span instead of staring at the whole run. Going down the tree is the correct move.

The problem is which child it picks. The run took 9 seconds. `plan` took only 1 of those seconds. Even if you made `plan` instant, the run would still take about 8 seconds. You would be fixing the wrong step.

The rule is to follow the **slowest** child down. That chain of slowest steps is the **critical path**: the steps that decide how long the whole run takes. `plan` is not on it. It ties with `write` as the fastest child.

The search tool took 7 of the 9 seconds. That is most of the run. Opening that span next might show something like a slow web request inside it, and that is where a fix would really pay off.

"Inside the search tool span" is better because search is the slowest child, so it is where the run's time actually went.

check:1:2.q: Why not “At the write step's prompt”?
check:1:2.a:
"At the write step's prompt" picks a real place to look. A prompt is the text you send to the model, and a long or messy one can slow a model call down. So the instinct to look inside a step is a good one.

The problem is which step. Write took 1 second out of 9. Even if you made it instant, the run would still take 8 seconds. That fix barely moves the total.

The lesson's rule is to start at the root (the top span, the whole run) and follow the slowest child down. Here the children are plan at 1 second, search at 7 seconds, and write at 1 second. Search is the slowest by far. It is the next step on the critical path, the chain of slowest steps from the top down.

"Inside the search tool span" is better because search holds 7 of the 9 seconds, so that is where the real delay lives, likely in a web request inside it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Count how many spans each helper made”?
check:2:0.a:
Counting spans gets one thing right. Because each helper is traced under its own name, you can group spans by helper. So you are looking at the right tree.

But a count tells you how many steps a helper took, not how long they took. Those are different things.

Picture this. The planner makes 12 spans, each a quick model call of about 50 ms. That is 600 ms in total. The researcher makes just 2 spans, but one is a web request that takes 3 seconds. Counting points you at the planner. The real holdup is the researcher.

Many small steps can be fast. One big step can be slow. A count can't tell these apart, because it ignores the `ms` on each span. That is the time each step took.

So the right option is "Follow the slowest child from the top." It is better because it uses time, not number of steps: starting at the team's top span and always stepping into the slowest child leads you straight to the helper, and the single call, that held the run up.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Compare how long each helper's reply is”?
check:2:1.a:
Comparing reply lengths has a grain of sense. A model writes its answer piece by piece, so a very long reply does take longer to produce. A helper that writes pages of text might be a little slower than one that writes a line.

But reply length measures how much text came out, not how long the helper took. Most of the waiting often happens before any text appears: tool calls, web requests, or several model calls in a row. A researcher could give a short summary after a 3-second web search. A writer could produce a long draft in under a second. Judging by length, you would blame the writer, and you would be wrong.

The trace already records real time for every span, so there is no need to guess from a side clue. (A span is one recorded step in the run.)

"Follow the slowest child from the top" is the better answer because it uses the measured times to go straight from the whole team run to the helper, and the step inside it, that actually took the longest.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. The claim about where waiting happens and the 'long draft in under a second' example come from outside the lesson and are a bit unrealistic, but they don't contradict it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the trace was read wrong**

- **You "fix" a step and the run is no faster.** The root span's total time barely moves. You probably blamed a parent for time that really belonged to one of its children. In the lesson's example, `tool:search` looks slow at 3100 ms, but `http_get` inside it takes 2900 ms. The web request is the real culprit.
- **The "slowest span" is always the root.** If you rank every span in one flat list, the top span wins every time, because it contains everything. That tells you nothing.
- **An agent team shows one big blob.** If helpers aren't traced under their own names, you see one long span with no children. You can't tell which helper held things up.
- **Own times don't add up.** A parent's time should be at least the sum of its children's times. If it isn't, spans may be attached to the wrong parent.

**Quickest check**

Take the span you blamed. Subtract its children's times from its total. If little is left, look one level deeper. After your fix, rerun and confirm the root's time dropped by about what you saved.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The one soft spot is the claim that a parent's time should be at least the sum of its children's times. It follows from the lesson's 'parent includes children' idea but is not stated outright.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The parent's own time is the biggest part.**
Say a parent takes 4000 ms but its children add up to only 1000 ms. The slow work is then inside the parent itself, so following a child sends you the wrong way. At each step, subtract the children's time from the parent's time first, and stop at the parent if its own time is the largest.

**2. Many small steps instead of one slow one.**
An agent might call a tool ten times in a row, 300 ms each. No single call looks slow, yet together they take 3000 ms. Count how many times each step repeats and add up their times, because the fix may be making fewer calls.

**3. One trace is only one run.**
A web request can be slow once by bad luck, like a busy network. That one trace may blame a step that is usually fast. Look at many traces and see which step is slow most often before you change anything.

learn:term.a:
A **trace** is the whole record of one agent run. A **span** is one timed step inside that run.

So a trace is made of spans. One run gives you one trace. That trace holds many spans: the run itself, each model call, each tool call, each web request.

Spans nest. A span can sit inside another span. The outer one is the **parent**. The ones directly inside it are its **children**. Put together, they form a tree, and that whole tree is the trace.

Everyday comparison: a trace is like the receipt for one shopping trip. Each line on the receipt is a span. Some lines group others, like a "Groceries" heading with items listed under it.

In the lesson's example, the whole tree is one trace. `agent_run`, `plan`, `tool:search`, `http_get` and `answer` are five spans. `http_get` (2900 ms) is a child of `tool:search` (3100 ms). So the search span's own time is just 200 ms.

Short version: the trace is the full story, and the spans are the steps in it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Nothing: MLflow can work out the config afterwa…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. MLflow does record a lot on its own: inputs, outputs, timings and token counts for every step.

But the config isn't one of those things. A config is a choice you made, like which settings or prompt version a request ran with. A trace has no way to show that choice unless your code writes it down. Two requests from different configs can look almost the same in the trace.

So if last week's traces were saved without a config tag, MLflow has nothing to sort them by. A search like this would find nothing:

```python
mlflow.search_traces(filter_string="tag.config = 'cs512-k5'")
```

A "tag" here is a small label, a name and a value, stuck onto the trace. You can't go back and add the right label later, because nothing in the trace tells you which config it came from. As the lesson says, if it isn't in the traces when they're created, no analysis later can recover it.

"Each trace was tagged with its config at the time" is better because the label was attached while the request ran. So every trace can be sorted into the right pile and compared.

judge.notes: Minor: it says nothing in the trace can reveal the config, which slightly overstates the lesson (span inputs like k are recorded). It is also close to the 200-word limit and uses two sentences where one was asked for the 'better' option.

check:0:2.q: Why not “You built a new eval set from that week's traff…”?
check:0:2.a:
Building an eval set from last week's traffic isn't wrong in itself. An **eval set** is a fixed list of test questions, sometimes with expected answers. Pulling real questions from production makes a good one, and you could later run both configs on it.

But it misses what the question asks. You want to compare the two configs on what *actually happened* last week. That means you need to know which config answered each real request. An eval set holds the questions. It doesn't record which config served them.

That fact can only be captured at the moment each trace is created. If no `config` tag was saved then, it's gone. No amount of later work can recover it. You can't sort last week's traces into "config A" and "config B" piles without it.

Also, an eval set is something you build afterwards. The question asks what must *already* be true.

"Each trace was tagged with its config at the time" is better because it's the only option that lets you split last week's real traces by config and compare them directly.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the eval-set definition comes from outside the lesson but is accurate, and the answer comes in just under the word limit.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Read the 10 newest traces one by one”?
check:1:0.a:
Reading the 10 newest traces one by one gets one thing right: you are looking at real data. Opening a single trace is also a good way to spot something odd, like one slow retrieval step.

But it can't answer "did the new prompt make answers slower?" Here's why:

- **Ten is too few.** Response times jump around from question to question. A few long questions can make a version look slow when it isn't.
- **"Newest" isn't the same as "new prompt."** The 10 most recent traces might all be the new version. Then you have nothing to compare against. Or they might be a random mix, and you'd have to sort them in your head.
- **It ignores the tags.** You tagged every trace with its prompt version for exactly this kind of question. Reading by date throws that work away.
- **It's hard to repeat.** Eyeballing timings by hand is slow, and two people might come away with different answers.

"Group by prompt version, compare times" is better because it uses every tagged trace and puts each version's average time side by side, so the comparison is fair and the answer is clear.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Average the time across all traces”?
check:1:2.a:
Averaging the time across all traces gets one thing right: it measures time, which is what you care about. It gives you a real number for how slow the app is overall.

But it mixes every trace into one pile. Traces from the old prompt and traces from the new prompt all go into the same average. So you get a single number that blends both versions together. You can't tell whether the new prompt made things slower, because nothing in that number separates old from new.

It also hides the size of any change. Say the new prompt is much slower but only a small share of traces used it. The overall average barely moves, and you might wrongly decide nothing changed.

This is why you tag traces in the first place. The prompt version tag is already sitting on every trace. Averaging across everything throws that tag away and ignores the very thing you set up to answer this question.

"Group by prompt version, compare times" is better because it gives each version its own average, so you can put the old and new numbers side by side and see the difference directly.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The model name on each trace”?
check:2:0.a:
Tagging each trace with the model name is a good habit. The lesson recommends it. A tag is a label you attach to a whole trace, so you can later split results by model, like comparing `fast-model` against another one.

But it doesn't solve this problem. The question is about finding retrieval steps *inside* each trace. A trace holds many spans, one per step: a model call, a retrieval, a tool. A model name tag sits on the whole trace, so every span in that trace shares the same label. It tells you which model ran the request. It doesn't tell you which span fetched documents. Your evaluation would still have to guess.

The fix belongs on the spans themselves. Marking a span with a type, like `span_type="RETRIEVER"` in `@mlflow.trace(span_type="RETRIEVER")`, labels that exact step as a retrieval. Evaluation and analysis tools can then pick it out directly.

"A RETRIEVER type on those spans" is better because it labels each retrieval step itself, so your evaluation can find every one without guessing.

judge.notes: Minor: saying 'every span shares the same label' slightly overstates how a trace-level tag works, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:2:1.q: Why not “A longer name for each span”?
check:2:1.a:
A longer name isn't wrong in spirit. A name like `retrieve_docs_from_vector_store` does tell a human what the step does. Reading one trace by eye, that helps.

But your evaluation isn't a human reading names. It's code that has to find every retrieval step, in every trace, automatically.

Names are free text. Each person picks their own. One function is `retrieve`, another is `search_kb`, and a LangGraph node might be called `fetch`. To find them all, you'd have to guess words to search for. Then it breaks the day someone renames a function.

A span type is different. It's a fixed label from a short, agreed list (`RETRIEVER`, `TOOL`, `CHAT_MODEL`). MLflow and its evaluation tools already know to look for it. So "find all retrieval steps" becomes one exact match, not a guess.

```python
@mlflow.trace(span_type="RETRIEVER")
def search_kb(question, k):
    ...
```

The name here doesn't matter. The type still says "this is a retrieval."

A `RETRIEVER` type is better because it's a standard label that tools can reliably find, whatever each span happens to be called.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Log what the model saw” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When an answer is wrong, the question is always "why?" You can only answer that if you can see exactly what the model was given. That means the full prompt (the text sent to the model), the retrieved chunks (the pieces of documents your search pulled in), and every tool call with its inputs and outputs.

If you don't log these, you're left guessing. Was the model confused? Did the search fetch the wrong documents? Did a tool return an error? Each cause needs a different fix. Without the evidence, you might change the prompt when the real problem was retrieval.

A small example. A user asks, "What's our refund window?" The app says 14 days, but the policy says 30. With a trace, you open that request and see the retriever returned last year's policy document. Now you know to fix the document index, not the model.

Without the trace, you can't recover that moment. You can rerun the question, but the documents or data may have changed since. The original cause is gone. That's why you record it when the request happens.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Filters come back short.** You search for one version's traces and get far fewer than you expected, or none at all.
- **Piles that shouldn't exist.** One version shows up under two names, like `fast-model` and `Fast-Model`. Its results get split, so each pile looks smaller and noisier than it really is.
- **Retrieval scores are blank.** Evaluations that check retrieved documents find nothing. Usually the retrieval step was never marked with the `RETRIEVER` span type. A span is one step inside a trace.
- **Versions won't line up.** You can't put v1 and v2 side by side question by question. Often `mlflow.set_active_model` was never called, so traces aren't linked to a named version.

**Quickest check**

Pick a time window. Count every trace in it. Then count the traces for each value of the `config` tag separately, and add those counts together. The sum should equal the total. If it's smaller, some traces are missing the tag.

While you're there, read the list of tag values and look for typos. Then open one trace and confirm each step has the right span type.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The answer is about 180 words, and the signs and the count-and-sum check follow from the lesson's tags, span types and set_active_model.

learn:stops.a:
Grouping by a tag and averaging works well, but here are three places it needs care.

**Tags missing or spelled differently.** Traces recorded before you added tags get skipped, and `fast-model` versus `Fast-Model` splits one version into two piles. Set tags in one place from your config, and check how many traces landed in each pile before trusting the averages.

**A few slow requests skew the average.** One timeout or retry can drag a version's average up, especially when a pile has only a handful of traces. Also look at the median (the middle value) and the slowest 5% of requests. Collect enough traces per version before drawing conclusions.

**Versions saw different traffic.** If v2 ran in production on harder questions while v1 ran on a test set, the comparison is unfair. Tag `environment` and compare only within one environment. Better still, run both versions on the same fixed question set, linked with `mlflow.set_active_model`, so you can line them up question by question.

learn:term.a:
Both are tags, meaning labels you attach to a trace so you can split results later. They answer different questions.

**`model`** says *which language model* produced the answer. In the lesson's LangGraph example it's `ENDPOINT`, the model serving endpoint (the web address your app calls to reach the model). In the first example it's `"fast-model"`.

**`config`** says *how the rest of your app was set up* around that model. It names a bundle of settings. The lesson's value is `"cs512-k5"`. The `k5` part matches `retrieve(question, k=5)`, so it likely means "fetch 5 documents." The lesson doesn't say what `cs512` stands for. It's just part of the name your team picked for that setup.

Think of a coffee shop. The `model` is the coffee bean. The `config` is the brewing recipe. Change either one and the cup tastes different.

Tagging both lets you separate the two causes. Keep `config` fixed and swap `model`, and any difference comes from the model. Keep `model` fixed and change `config`, and you're testing your setup. Without both tags, you couldn't tell which change made things better or worse.

judge.notes: No major problems. The tutor's reading of config (a bundle of app settings) and its guess that k5 means 5 documents go beyond what the lesson says, but it hedges the guess and admits the lesson doesn't explain cs512.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Check that each summary is under 500 words”?
check:0:0.a:
A word limit only tells you how long the summary is. In this Check question, the runs are already shorter, so length isn't the problem. The problem is that the agent rewrites a table it already wrote.

A summary can be well under 500 words and still leave out the table name. The lesson's example shows this. "Fix the HR tickets. Next: rerun the job." is very short. Yet when asked "Which table did we write to?", the agent says "I'm not sure." A length check would pass that summary. It can't see what got dropped.

The lesson's rule is to judge a summary by whether the agent can still finish the task, not by how short it is. Counting words measures shortness, so it tests the wrong thing.

**Plant facts, compact, then ask probe questions** is the right answer. You hide details like a table name in a long run. You compact it, which means swapping old messages for a summary. Then you ask about those details.

That approach is better because it directly checks whether the agent still remembers the exact details it needs, like which table it wrote, so it catches the forgetting that causes the repeated work.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Ask the model whether its summary looks complete”?
check:0:1.a:
Asking the model "does your summary look complete?" sounds sensible. It is cheap, and it might catch an obvious gap, like a missing "next step" section.

But it has two big problems.

First, the model is grading its own work. Models tend to say "yes, looks good." A summary can read smoothly and still be missing the one detail that matters.

Second, it never tests the actual failure. The bug here is that the agent rewrites a table it already wrote. That happens because the exact table name was dropped during **compaction** (swapping old messages for a short summary). "Looks complete" is a feeling, not a check. Nobody asks, "Which table did we write to?" So nobody finds out the agent can't answer.

You also get no number. You can't compare two summary prompts, or see if a change made things better or worse.

That is why "Plant facts, compact, then ask probe questions" is the right answer. You hide known details in the run, then directly ask about each one, so you get a real count of what survived the summary.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Summarise everything into one line”?
check:1:0.a:
"Summarise everything into one line" does get one thing right. It makes the context much smaller, so the agent has room to keep going.

The problem is what gets lost. A one-line summary is the vague kind the lesson warns about. Exact details like table names, ticket ids and error codes get dropped. The lesson's example shows this: the summary says "Fix the HR tickets. Next: rerun the job." Then the probe question "Which table did we write to?" gets "I'm not sure." An agent that forgets details like that may redo work, or say it is finished when it is not.

It is also the wrong place to start. The lesson says to try the cheap fix first. Only if runs are still too long should you summarise. Even then, the summary should have required sections: the goal, decisions, exact names, ids and error codes, open tasks and the next step. The last few messages should stay word for word.

"Clear old tool results, keep a note" is better because it is the cheaper first step: it only swaps out old tool outputs, leaving a note that each tool ran.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Switch off the tools for the run”?
check:1:2.a:
"Switch off the tools for the run" spots something true. Tool results are often the biggest thing filling the context. The context is everything the model can see at once. A single database query can return thousands of lines, and those pile up fast.

But switching tools off throws away the agent's hands. Tools are how it reads tables, runs jobs and updates tickets. Without them, it can talk about the task but cannot do it. Remember the lesson's rule: judge a fix by whether the agent can still finish the task. This one fails that test straight away.

It also does nothing about the old results already sitting in the context. The space is still used up.

Clearing old tool results is gentler. The agent keeps its tools. Only old outputs get swapped for a short `[cleared]` note, and the newest few stay in full. In the lesson's code, `ClearToolUsesEdit(trigger=60000, keep=3)` does exactly this.

"Clear old tool results, keep a note" is better because it frees up space while the agent keeps working and still knows which tools already ran, so it won't redo them.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims that tool results are often the biggest context filler and that one query can return thousands of lines go beyond the lesson, but they are plausible and do not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “A, because it saves more room”?
check:2:0.a:
Option A has a fair point. Saving room matters. The context window is how much text the model can see at once. A shorter summary leaves more space for new work, and it costs fewer tokens (the small chunks of text that models count and charge for).

But room is not the goal. A summary exists so the agent can keep going and finish the task. If prompt A makes summaries half as long, it probably cut something. Often it is the exact details: a table name, a ticket id, an error code. Those are the first things a vague summary drops.

When those details go missing, the agent pays for it later. It might redo work it already did. It might write to the wrong table. Or it might say it is finished when it is not. Any space you saved gets spent again, and the task may still fail.

That is why the lesson says to judge a summary by results, not by length.

B is better because a summary's real job is to keep what the agent needs to finish, and more finished tasks shows it did that job.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Neither, summaries are always vague”?
check:2:1.a:
"Neither, summaries are always vague" gets one thing right. A vague prompt like "summarise this" really does drop exact details, such as table names, ticket ids and error codes. The lesson's example shows it: after compaction, the agent can't say which table it wrote to.

But it misses two things.

First, vagueness is not fixed. Compaction (swapping old messages for a short summary) is often needed once the context fills up, so the useful question is how to make it better. A prompt with required sections asks for the goal, decisions, exact names, ids and error codes, open tasks and the next step. That makes keeping details more likely. It doesn't guarantee it, so you still test, for example with planted facts and probe questions.

Second, the question gives you evidence: with prompt B, the agent finishes more of its tasks. Saying "neither" throws that evidence away.

"B, because the agent still finishes" is better because the lesson says to judge a summary by whether the agent can still finish the task, not by how short it is.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Tell the summary what it must keep” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
A summary is written by a model. If you only say "summarise the chat", it keeps the general idea and drops the specifics. To the model, "we wrote to a table" sounds like enough. But the agent needs the exact name to carry on.

**Example:** an agent is fixing HR tickets. It wrote cleaned rows to `hr_tickets_clean` and is working on ticket `HR-4821`. The context fills up, so it gets compacted, meaning the old messages are swapped for a summary: "Fix the HR tickets. Next: rerun the job."

Now the agent can't say which table it used. It might write to a new table, redo the cleaning, or pick the wrong ticket. Worse, it might decide it is finished because the summary sounds tidy.

So spell out what the summary must keep:

- the goal
- decisions made
- exact names, ids and error codes
- open tasks
- the next step

Then test it with a probe question. That is a question about a detail you know was in the run, like "Which table did we write to?" If the agent can't answer, the summary lost something the agent needed.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that compaction is losing details**

Trouble usually shows up right after compaction. Compaction is the moment old messages get swapped for a summary. Look in your traces (the step-by-step record of each run) just after that point.

- **Repeated work.** The agent calls the same tool again with the same inputs, because it forgot the first result.
- **Fuzzy or invented details.** A table name, ticket id or error code is missing, slightly wrong, or made up.
- **Early "done".** The agent says it has finished while open tasks remain.
- **Questions it already had answers to.** It asks the user for something given earlier in the run.

Watch your numbers too. Short test runs may look perfect because they never get long enough to compact. Then real, longer runs fail more often. A summary that is very short and tidy is also a warning sign. Short is not the same as useful.

**Quickest check**

Take one long run and plant three or four exact facts in it. Force a compaction. Then ask a probe question about each fact, such as "Which ticket id are we fixing?" Count how many come back exactly right. Any miss means your summary prompt needs a required section for that kind of detail.

judge.notes: No real problems. It is about 208 words, which is borderline on length, and it adds a few plausible signs the lesson does not state (invented details, re-asking the user).

learn:stops.a:
**When planted-fact testing needs extra care**

**1. Facts change during the run.** Say the agent writes to `hr_tickets`, then switches to `hr_tickets_v2`. A summary that keeps the old name looks right but sends the agent to the wrong place. Plant the update too, and score against the latest value only.

**2. Answers are right but worded differently.** The agent might reply "the hr_tickets table" when you planted `hr_tickets`. A strict word-for-word match counts that as forgotten. Clean up answers first, for example by lowercasing and trimming extra words, or use a second model as a judge (a model that just grades whether the answer means the same thing).

**3. Many compactions in one long run.** Each summary gets summarised again, so small losses pile up. Run your probes after the third or fourth compaction, not just the first. For facts that must never be lost, save them outside the chat, such as in a notes file the agent reads back.

learn:term.a:
Think of a long meeting. Someone writes notes so a latecomer can catch up without replaying the whole recording. Compacting is writing those notes.

An agent's **context** is everything the model can see at once: your messages, its replies and tool results. It has a size limit, measured in **tokens** (small chunks of text, roughly pieces of words). When the context gets too full, the agent compacts it. It swaps the old messages for a short summary and carries on.

The risk is the same as with bad meeting notes. If the summary is vague, exact details vanish.

In the lesson's example, the long run held three planted facts: the goal, a table name and a ticket id. After compacting, the summary only said "Fix the HR tickets. Next: rerun the job." The goal roughly survived. The table name and ticket id did not. So when asked "Which table did we write to?", the agent answered "I'm not sure."

In the LangChain code, `SummarizationMiddleware` does the compacting. Past 100000 tokens, it summarises older messages and keeps the last 20 word for word.

judge.notes: No real problems. The remark that the goal 'roughly survived' is a mild inference, since the lesson only marks the table as forgotten, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Record only 1 run in 10, and judge those”?
check:0:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. Judging, which means asking a model to read a trace and score it, is the expensive part. Doing it for only 1 run in 10 really does cut the cost.

The mistake is applying the "1 in 10" to recording too. Recording a trace is cheap. It just saves what happened. If you only record 1 run in 10, the other 9 are gone for good.

That hurts in a few ways:

- A failing run is often rare. It may well land in the 9 you threw away.
- A user reports a bad answer, and there is no trace to open.
- Your trace table is missing rows. Sorting by steps or tool errors can't surface a run that was never saved.
- You can't go back later and judge the runs you skipped.

So you keep paying for agent runs but lose the evidence you need most.

"Record every run, and judge only 1 in 10" is better because you still save on the expensive judging, while every trace stays available to sort, filter and open when something goes wrong.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the claim that recording is cheap is not in the lesson but is consistent with it.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Judge only the runs users complained about”?
check:0:1.a:
"Judge only the runs users complained about" gets two things right. Complaints point you at real problems. And judging fewer runs does save money. Here, "judging" means having a model score how good a run was.

But it misses a lot. If you only judge complaints, you only see the failures someone chose to report. A bad run can still slip by with no complaint. It might take nine steps, hit four tool errors, or come close to filling the context window. That is the most text a model can read in one call. The run could still end with an answer nobody flags, and you would never look at it.

You also lose your view of normal runs. If you never judge ordinary runs, you can't tell whether quality is getting better or worse overall.

"Record every run, and judge only 1 in 10" is better. It keeps every trace for later digging and cuts judging costs to a tenth. It also checks a steady slice of all runs, not just the ones someone reported.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The ones with the fewest tokens”?
check:1:0.a:
"The ones with the fewest tokens" has one small grain of truth. A run with very few tokens (tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes) can mean it stopped early, maybe because something broke on the first step. So a tiny number is not always good news.

Most of the time, though, few tokens just means a short, simple run. The agent asked one question, got an answer and finished. Those are usually the runs that went fine. Reading them first spends your time on the boring cases.

Trouble tends to show up as size and struggle, not smallness. An agent that is stuck often loops: it calls the model again and again, retries tools and piles up tokens. A token count only tells you how big a run was. It does not say whether anything went wrong.

"The ones with many steps or tool errors" is better because those two numbers point straight at runs where the agent struggled or something actually failed, so they are the runs most likely to teach you something.

judge.notes: The 'stopped early' grain of truth and the claim that short runs usually went fine are not in the lesson, but they do not contradict it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The first 20 rows in the table”?
check:1:2.a:
"The first 20 rows" gets one thing right. It keeps your reading to a small, doable number. Nobody can read 2,000 traces, so picking a handful is the right instinct.

The problem is *which* handful. The order of rows in a table usually has nothing to do with quality. It might be the order the runs happened, or the order of their `trace_id` (the label each trace gets). So the first 20 rows are close to a random pick. Most runs are fine, so those 20 will probably be ordinary, healthy runs. The few broken ones could sit at row 1,437, and you'd never see them.

It also skips the reason you built the table. You turned each trace into numbers so you could **sort and filter** them, like a spreadsheet. Taking the top 20 without sorting first throws that advantage away.

"The ones with many steps or tool errors" is better because sorting by those numbers puts the runs most likely to have gone wrong at the top, so your limited reading time goes to the runs that matter.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The run made too many tool calls”?
check:2:1.a:
"The run made too many tool calls" has a small grain of truth. Each tool result is usually pasted back into the prompt for the next model call, so lots of tool calls can make prompts grow. That is one possible cause.

But the biggest prompt doesn't measure tool calls. It is the most input tokens in any single model call. Tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads. The number tells you how much text the model had to read in one go. It doesn't say why. A huge prompt could come from one long document, a long chat history, or a single tool that returned a wall of text. The row has no column that counts tool calls, so you can't read "too many tool calls" from it.

The context window is the most a model can read in one call. A biggest prompt near that limit means the run was close to hitting it. Past the limit, text gets cut off or the call fails.

"The run nearly ran out of room" is better because it states exactly what the number measures: how close one call came to filling the context window.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that text is cut off or the call fails past the limit goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and the answer is about 195 words, just under the limit.

check:2:2.q: Why not “The run cost less than usual”?
check:2:2.a:
"The run cost less than usual" points the wrong way. A big prompt means many input tokens. Tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads and writes, and you pay per token. So a huge prompt usually makes a run cost **more**, not less.

It does get one thing right. Token counts and cost are linked. But cost is better read from the `total` column, which adds up the tokens from every call in the run.

The biggest prompt, the `peak` column, answers a different question. It is the most input tokens in any **single** call. You compare it with the context window, which is the most text a model can read in one call. When `peak` sits close to that limit, the run was nearly too big for the model. One more long tool result could have pushed it over. Then the model would fail, or older text would get cut off.

"The run nearly ran out of room" is better because the biggest prompt measures how full one call got, compared with the most that call can hold.

judge.notes: No check fails, but 'you pay per token' and 'the model would fail, or older text would get cut off' are not in the lesson; they are true in general but go beyond it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs this went wrong**

- **You are still reading traces one by one.** After a few dozen runs you miss the bad ones. Users report failures you never saw.
- **The errors column is always 0**, yet logs or users show tools failing. Something is not being counted.
- **Every row looks fine**, but quality drops in real use. This often means traces were *recorded* only for a sample, so the failing runs were never kept. Keep every trace. Sample only the judging.
- **Peak and total look odd.** If peak is larger than total, the numbers are mixed up. If total equals peak on runs with many steps, tokens from the other calls were dropped.
- **Runs that hit the context window** (the most a model can read in one call) show a small peak. The biggest prompt is being missed.
- **Empty traces break the table** or show strange values instead of zeros.

**Quickest check**

Pick one trace you know failed. Open it and count by hand: model calls, failed tool calls, the largest single input, and all tokens added up. Compare with its row. If they differ, fix the counting before trusting any sort or filter.

judge.notes: No clear problem. The 'often means' claim about sampling is slightly strong, and the answer sits right at the ~200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where turning each trace into a row of numbers needs extra care.

**1. Quiet failures.** A run can take two steps, hit no tool errors and still give a wrong answer. The numbers only show effort and trouble, not whether the answer was correct. So also judge a sample of runs for quality, using a person or an "LLM judge" (a model asked to grade answers), even when their rows look calm.

**2. Much bigger systems.** If one trace covers several agents working together, a single row blends them all. You can't tell which agent caused the errors. Add columns for each agent, or make one row per agent per run, so sorting still points to the right place.

**3. Things change over time.** After you switch models or edit a prompt, "normal" step counts and token use shift. A new model may also have a bigger or smaller context window, which changes what a high "biggest prompt" means. Compare rows against recent runs on the same setup, not against old fixed limits.

judge.notes: No real problems. It stays under 200 words, gives three cases with fixes, and does not contradict the lesson. It skips the lesson's own caveat that sampling can discard failing runs, and "agents" is left unexplained, but both are minor.

learn:term.a:
Think of a big filing cabinet. Every folder has an address: which cabinet, which drawer, which folder. Unity Catalog is Databricks' version of that for data. It holds tables, and each table has a three-part name: `catalog.schema.table`. A catalog is the top level. A schema is a group inside it. A table is the data itself.

In this lesson, Unity Catalog is where production traces can be stored as tables. Then you can query them with SQL, the standard language for asking questions of tables. For example: "show runs with more than 3 tool errors."

Why bother? Traces kept only in an MLflow experiment (MLflow's own space for tracking runs) stop at 100,000. Unity Catalog tables have no limit. That is why Databricks recommends it for production.

In the code comment, reading those traces takes two steps. First, set `MLFLOW_TRACING_SQL_WAREHOUSE_ID` to a SQL warehouse id. A SQL warehouse is the Databricks computing power that runs SQL queries. Then add `locations=["catalog.schema"]` to `mlflow.search_traces`. That points the search at the right drawer of the cabinet.
